'''Jerome Kalman Sherman''' (August 14, 1925 – December 1, 2023) was an American biologist and credited as a founder of modern [[sperm bank]]ing and cryopreservation. Sherman was also a professor of biology at [[University of Arkansas]] for more than three decades.<ref name=":4" />

== Early life and military service ==
Jerome Kalman Sherman was born in 1925 in [[Brooklyn|Brooklyn, New York]], to Murray and Beatrice Sherman, a sailmaker and Navy Yard worker. After graduating from [[Erasmus Hall High School]] early,<ref name=":02">{{Cite web |date=2013-02-17 |title=Jerome Kalman Sherman |url=https://www.arkansasonline.com/news/2013/feb/17/jerome-kalman-sherman-20130217/ |access-date=2023-04-25 |website=Arkansas Online |language=en}}</ref> he enrolled at [[Brooklyn College]] at the age of 16, but after three semesters put his studies on hold to enlist in the military during World War II.

At age 17, in 1943, Sherman joined the [[United States Navy|U.S. Navy]] as a seaman and earned a commission at Notre Dame. He then served in the [[Pacific War|Pacific Theater]] as an anti-submarine officer until 1945, learning of the Japanese surrender on his 20th birthday. Subsequently he served in occupied Japan as part of the first naval line officer to enter Nagasaki, left the Navy as a lieutenant commander.<ref name=":2">{{Cite web |title=Encyclopedia of Arkansas |url=https://encyclopediaofarkansas.net/entries/jerome-kalman-sherman-8019/ |access-date=2023-04-25 |website=Encyclopedia of Arkansas |language=en-US}}</ref>

== Education ==
Sherman received his bachelor's degree in biology in 1947 from [[Brown University]]. In 1949 he received a master's degree in biology from [[Case Western Reserve University|Western Reserve University]] (now [[Case Western Reserve University|Case Western University]]). He completed his graduate studies at the [[University of Iowa]], where he earned a doctorate in zoology in 1954.<ref name=":12">{{Cite web |title=DAA Awardee: Jerome K. Sherman {{!}} University of Iowa Center for Advancement |url=https://www.foriowa.org/daa/daa-profile.php?namer=true&profileid=460 |access-date=2023-04-25 |website=www.foriowa.org |language=en}}</ref>

Sherman's doctoral thesis and research activity initially focused on electron microscopy, and later freezing kidney tissue;<ref name=":3">{{Cite web |last=Madrigal |first=Alexis C. |date=2014-04-28 |title=The Surprising Birthplace of the First Sperm Bank |url=https://www.theatlantic.com/technology/archive/2014/04/how-the-first-sperm-bank-began/361288/ |access-date=2023-05-02 |website=The Atlantic |language=en}}</ref> but he ultimately changed his subject to freezing and freeze-drying human semen after a series of successful trials in the university's urology department and fertility clinic.<ref name=":2" />

== Career and research ==
While a graduate student at the [[University of Iowa]], Sherman also worked in the campus library and as a janitor in addition to his research assistant duties.<ref name=":02" />

In 1953, while working as a research associate in the university's Department of Urology, Sherman refined a process that had been developed in 1949 by A.S. Parkes and two British scientists, which involved the use of glycerol to preserve animal sperm during freezing and thawing. Combined with the glycerol method, Sherman introduced slow cooling and use of solid carbon dioxide as a refrigerant during storage.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Sperm Banking History {{!}} California Cryobank |url=https://www.cryobank.com/learning-center/sperm-banking-101/sperm-banking-history/ |access-date=2023-04-25 |website=www.cryobank.com}}</ref> Sherman collaborated on these experiments with urologist Dr. Raymond Bunge, who arranged for Sherman to be hired in the urology department and who was affiliated with the university's new fertility clinic, which had opened in early 1952.<ref name=":4">Swanson, Kara W. "The Birth of the Sperm Bank." The Annals of Iowa 71 (2012), 241-276. Available at: https://doi.org/10.17077/0003-4827.1645</ref> Bunge and Sherman had met while Sherman was painting the former's house in another side job.<ref name=":2" />

In 1953, three patients at the clinic were impregnated using frozen sperm, with Dr. William Keettel, an obstetrician at the fertility clinic, overseeing the patients. The same year, Sherman established the first sperm cryobank in the world in [[Iowa City, Iowa|Iowa City]] to assist these pregnancies.<ref>{{Cite web |title=First cryobank for frozen semen; first human pregnancy from frozen sperm. {{!}} Carver College of Medicine |url=https://medicine.uiowa.edu/content/first-cryobank-frozen-semen-first-human-pregnancy-frozen-sperm |access-date=2023-05-03 |website=medicine.uiowa.edu |archive-date=May 3, 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230503004425/https://medicine.uiowa.edu/content/first-cryobank-frozen-semen-first-human-pregnancy-frozen-sperm |url-status=dead }}</ref> Bunge and Sherman published their findings first in the [[Experimental Biology and Medicine (Society for Experimental Biology and Medicine journal)|Proceedings of the Society for Experimental Biology and Medicine]] and later ''[[Nature (journal)|Nature]]'' magazine.<ref name=":3" /><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Bunge |first1=R. G. |last2=Sherman |first2=J. K. |date=October 1953 |title=Fertilizing Capacity of Frozen Human Spermatozoa |url=https://www.nature.com/articles/172767b0 |journal=Nature |language=en |volume=172 |issue=4382 |pages=767–768 |doi=10.1038/172767b0 |pmid=13111181 |bibcode=1953Natur.172..767B |issn=1476-4687|url-access=subscription }}</ref> The babies from this initial experiment were born in 1954, and the milestone was first publicized in the [[The Gazette (Cedar Rapids, Iowa)|''Cedar Rapids Gazette'']] under the headline "Fatherhood After Death Has Now Been Proved Possible."<ref name=":4" />

After receiving his doctorate, Sherman accepted a position at the Biological Research Institute with the American Foundation for Biological Research in [[Madison, Wisconsin]], in 1954.<ref name=":2" /> In 1957 Sherman joined the faculty at the [[University of Arkansas]]. He served as a professor there until 1992, when he became a professor emeritus and continued work until 1994. At [[University of Arkansas for Medical Sciences]], he founded what is considered to be the second human semen cryobank. During his career, he also traveled by request to assist with the establishment of other cryobanks across the country.<ref name=":02" /> He also helped to establish and advocate for the Office of Minority Affairs within the School of Medical Sciences at Arkansas.<ref name=":2" />

From 1974 to 1975, he spent a year on sabbatical teaching at [[National Chung Hsing University|National Chung-Hsing University]] in [[Taichung|Taichung, Taiwan]].<ref name=":02" /> Throughout his career, Sherman was also active in professional societies including his role as a charter member of the Society of Cryobiology in 1964, where he also served on the society's editorial board; as a founder of the American Association of Tissue Banks, where he drafted the first standards for the cryobanking of human embryos; and as an advisor to the [[Food and Drug Administration]] on AIDS and cryobanking from 1988 to 1992.<ref name=":2" />

== Personal life ==
Sherman met and married Hildegard Schroeder while they were both graduate students at the [[University of Iowa]], and they had three children: Karen, Marc, and Keith.<ref name=":02" /> In addition to his professional activities, he has participated in organizations such as the [[Boy Scouts of America]], the [[Jewish War Veterans of the United States of America|Jewish War Veterans]] organization, and the [[Lions Clubs International|Lions Club]].<ref name=":12" />

Sherman died on December 1, 2023, at the age of 98.<ref>{{cite web |title=Dr. Jerome Kalman Sherman |url=https://www.arkansasonline.com/obituaries/2023/dec/07/dr-jerome-sherman-2023-12-07-91192/ |website=arkansasonline.com |publisher=Arkansas Democrat Gazette |access-date=29 December 2023}}</ref>

== Awards ==
* Faculty Volunteer Service Award, University of Arkansas<ref name=":12" />
* Outstanding Service Award, Veterans Association (1989-2005)<ref name=":12" />
* Distinguished Faculty Award, University of Arkansas (1992)<ref name=":2" />
* Distinguished Service Award, American Association of Tissue Banks (1994)<ref name=":2" />
* Senior Arkansans Hall of Fame (1995)
* Silver Beaver Award, Boy Scouts of American (1998)
* Distinguished Alumni Award, University of Iowa (2006)<ref name=":12" />
